title: 4_Inequalities

findings.finding: The opening tasks rehearse reading supplied graphs, but do not rehearse obtaining intercepts from factors and constructing the cubic sketch used in the worked example.
findings.breakdown: Students can identify positive and negative regions on supplied graphs without recalling how factor signs determine roots or how the leading term determines end behaviour.
findings.checked: p3-a–p3-f supply graphs. p4-example-item uses factor-derived roots and positive-leading cubic end behaviour. No earlier topic supplies rehearsal. Repeated-root behaviour and negative-leading end behaviour are omitted from this finding because the worked example does not use them.
findings.assumptions: Polynomial sketching is prior course knowledge. No calculator is needed.

repair.proposal: Append three compact items to p3-identify-block: (i) Find the zeros of (x+3)(x-2)(x-5). Answer: -3, 2, 5. (ii) For y=(x+1)(x-2)(x-4), state the leading term and right-hand end behaviour. Answer: x³; y→∞ as x→∞. (iii) Sketch y=(x+1)(x-2)(x-4), labelling its x-intercepts. Answer: crossings at -1, 2, 4; left end falls and right end rises. Keep the complete review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: The opening review rehearses factor-derived roots and constructing a positive-leading cubic sketch before p4-example-item.

findings.finding: Compare all four inequality signs for a fixed cubic with a repeated zero.
findings.breakdown: The comparison distinguishes sign intervals from including an isolated touching zero.
findings.checked: For x²(x-4), the sign is negative below 4 except at zero, and positive above 4. All proposed answers are correct. Repeating q1e has an explicit comparison purpose. Existing practice does not contain this four-symbol run.
findings.assumptions: Students use the supplied graph of q1e for the comparison.

repair.proposal: After p5-q1f add the instruction: ‘Predict how each solution changes before solving.’ Add (g) x²(x-4)>0, answer x>4; (h) x²(x-4)≥0, answer x=0 or x≥4; (i) x²(x-4)<0, answer x<0 or 0<x<4; (j) x²(x-4)≤0, answer x≤4. Reuse q1e's graph for g–j. Follow with (k) -(x+2)²(x-1)>0, answer x<1, x≠-2, supplying its graph under the existing instruction. In g–j only the inequality symbol varies.

findings.doneWhen: The fixed-polynomial comparison is followed by one unpatterned task.

findings.finding: Compare all four inequality symbols for a fixed reciprocal expression.
findings.breakdown: The run separates inclusion of an equality point from exclusion of a denominator zero.
findings.checked: All answers are correct with x≠0, or x≠1 in the final part. p8-c–p8-d compare opposite inclusive inequalities but do not provide the proposed strict-versus-inclusive comparison.
findings.assumptions: The denominator-square method is available from p7–p8.

repair.proposal: Append to p9-q1-root: ‘Predict how the solution changes before solving each part.’ Add (d) 1/x>2, answer 0<x<1/2; (e) 1/x≥2, answer 0<x≤1/2; (f) 1/x<2, answer x<0 or x>1/2; (g) 1/x≤2, answer x<0 or x≥1/2. Follow with (h) 3/(x-1)≥2, answer 1<x≤5/2. In d–g only the comparison symbol varies.

findings.doneWhen: The four-symbol run retains the same expression and constant and ends with an unpatterned task.

findings.finding: Follow the existing reciprocal inequality with a comparison that exposes its equality case.
findings.breakdown: The repeated factor explains why the expression cannot fall below 2 on its positive domain.
findings.checked: x+1/x-2=(x-1)²/x for x≠0. It is negative for x<0, zero only at x=1, and otherwise positive for x>0. The proposed tasks use methods available by this topic's end.
findings.assumptions: The follow-up remains attached to p11-q4-h and uses its expression.

repair.proposal: After p11-q4-h add: (i) Solve x+1/x≤2. Answer: x<0 or x=1. (j) Solve x+1/x=2. Answer: x=1. (k) Explain why x+1/x cannot be less than 2 when x>0. Expected answer: x+1/x-2=(x-1)²/x≥0 when x>0.

findings.doneWhen: The follow-up contains separate numerical comparison, equality and explanation parts.

findings.finding: The topic has no opening rehearsal of negative-bracket expansion and solving a linear inequality with a negative coefficient, both used directly in p14-example-algebra.
findings.breakdown: The right-hand solution requires expanding -(2x-4) and reversing the inequality when dividing by -2 while students are learning how to combine absolute-value conditions.
findings.checked: p13 develops distance interpretation. The preceding rational topic and its supplied practice do not rehearse this negative-coefficient linear solution sequence. Ordinary rearrangement already occurs in p7–p8, so it is not retained as a separate missing piece.
findings.assumptions: These are previously learned linear-inequality skills. No calculator is needed.

repair.proposal: Before p13-investigation add: (a) Expand -(2x-5). Answer: -2x+5. (b) Solve -2x≤6. Answer: x≥-3. (c) Solve -3x+4>10. Answer: x<-2. Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: The review checks negative-bracket expansion and inequality reversal before the absolute-value worked example.

findings.finding: p18-q6-b and p18-q6-e repeat the whole task |4-x|≤0 without an explicit instructional purpose.
findings.breakdown: The later copy repeats the same stem, values and required solution.
findings.checked: Both complete tasks are identical, with no differing givens, diagrams or parts. No retrieval or comparison purpose is stated. The replacement has solution x=7/2.
findings.assumptions: No instructional purpose beyond the supplied text is inferred.
findings.doneWhen: The later copy retains the zero-bound structure with different numbers.

findings.finding: Reuse the two absolute-value graphs to compare inclusive and strict exterior solutions.
findings.breakdown: Students connect the reversed comparison with exterior intervals and track whether intersections belong.
findings.checked: The curves intersect at x=-2 and x=4/3. |2x-1| is greater outside those intersections and smaller between them. Both functions are defined for every real x, and the graphical method is already available.
findings.assumptions: Students retain the graphs drawn for the existing question.

repair.proposal: Append to p19-q10-root: (b) Hence solve |2x-1|≥|x-3|. Answer: x≤-2 or x≥4/3. (c) Solve |2x-1|>|x-3|. Answer: x<-2 or x>4/3.

findings.doneWhen: The follow-up uses the existing graphs for inclusive and strict exterior comparisons.

protectedGroups.observation: The same polynomial supports a deliberate comparison between non-negative and non-positive intervals.
protectedGroups.invariant: Polynomial, intercepts, curve and inclusion of equality.

protectedGroups.observation: A strict negative inequality excludes a touching zero even though the sign does not change there.
protectedGroups.varies: Root locations and a positive scalar multiplier.
protectedGroups.invariant: Positive-leading cubic, double smaller zero, simple larger zero and strict negative inequality.

protectedGroups.observation: Reversing the comparison switches the selected intervals while the denominator zero remains excluded.
protectedGroups.invariant: The rational expression, comparison constant and boundary values.

protectedGroups.observation: Distance conditions produce interior intervals or exterior rays around the same centre.
protectedGroups.varies: The inequality direction within each pair; the centre and coefficient across successive pairs.
protectedGroups.invariant: The absolute value expression and boundary magnitude within each pair.

protectedGroups.observation: Negating the expression inside absolute value preserves its magnitude and solution set; the explicit explanation justifies reusing p16-q2-h as the baseline.
protectedGroups.varies: The signs of both terms inside absolute value.
protectedGroups.invariant: The magnitude, comparison direction and threshold.

protectedGroups.observation: Non-negativity distinguishes all-real, one-excluded-value, empty and singleton solution sets.
Graphical comparison and restricted algebraic cases produce the same solution intervals.

importReview: Lean content review table: 37 of 37 blocks passed.

dropped.reason: The mathematics is correct, but this overlaps c2's stronger comparison of strict and inclusive solutions at a repeated zero. Drop it when selecting the four suggestions that best fit the booklet.

candidates.finding: Use the same cubic to distinguish an isolated equality solution from a sign interval.
